source_text: Τίς παρ' αὐταῖς τοὺς τῆς φιλοξενίας διώρισε νόμους; Τίς αὐταῖς ἠπείλησε λειποστρατίου γραφὴν, ὡς μηδεμίαν ἀπολείπεσθαι τῆς προπομπῆς. Ἀκουέ τωσαν οἱ κακόξενοι, καὶ τὰς θύρας κλείοντες, καὶ μηδὲ στέγης ἐν χειμῶνι καὶ νυκτὶ τοῖς ἐπιδημοῦσι μεταδιδόντες. Ἡ δὲ περὶ τοὺς γηράσαντας τῶν πελαργῶν πρόνοια ἐξήρκει τοὺς παῖδας ἡμῶν, εἰ προσέχειν ἐβούλοντο, φιλοπάτορας καταστῆσαι. Πάντως γὰρ οὐδεὶς οὕτως ἐλλείπων κατὰ τὴν φρόνησιν, ὡς μὴ αἰσχύνης ἄξιον κρίνειν τῶν ἀλογωτάτων ὀρνίθων ὑστερίζειν κατ' ἀρετήν. Ἐκεῖνοι τὸν πατέρα ὑπὸ τοῦ γήρως πτερορρυήσαντα περιστάντες ἐν κύκλῳ τοῖς οἰκείοις πτεροῖς διαθάλπουσι, καὶ τὰς τροφὰς ἀφθόνως παρασκευάζοντες, τὴν δυνατὴν καὶ ἐν τῇ πτήσει παρέχονται βοήθειαν, ἠρέμα τῷ πτερῷ κουφίζοντες ἑκατέρωθεν. Καὶ οὕτω τοῦτο παρὰ πᾶσι διαβεβόηται, ὥστε ἤδη τινὲς τὴν τῶν εὐεργετημάτων ἀντίδοσιν ἀντιπελάργωσιν ὀνομάζουσι. Μηδεὶς πενίαν ὀδυρέσθω· μηδὲ ἀπογινωσκέτω ἑαυτοῦ τὴν ζωὴν, ὁ μηδεμίαν οἴκοι περιουσίαν καταλιπὼν, πρὸς τὸ τῆς χελιδόνος εὐμήχανον ἀποβλέπων. Ἐκείνη γὰρ τὴν καλιὰν πηγνυμένη, τὰ μὲν κάρφη τῷ στόματι διακομίζει· πηλὸν δὲ τοῖς ποσὶν ἆραι μὴ δυναμένη, τὰ ἄκρα τῶν πτερῶν ὕδατι καταβρέξασα, εἶτα τῇ λεπτοτάτῃ κόνει ἐνειληθεῖσα, οὕτως ἐπινοεῖ τοῦ πηλοῦ τὴν χρείαν· καὶ κατὰ μικρὸν ἀλλήλοις τὰ κάρφη οἷον κόλλῃ τινὶ τῷ πηλῷ συνδήσασα, ἐν αὐτῇ τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἐκτρέφει· ὧν ἐάν τις ἐκκεντήσῃ τὰ ὄμματα, ἔχει τινὰ παρὰ τῆς φύσεως ἰατρικὴν, δι' ἧς πρὸς ὑγείαν ἐπανάγει τῶν ἐκγόνων τὰς ὄψεις. Ταῦτά σε νουθετείτω, μὴ διὰ πενίαν πρὸς κακουργίαν τρέπεσθαι· μηδὲ ἐν τοῖς χαλεπωτάτοις πάθεσι πᾶσαν ἐλπίδα ῥίψαντα, ἄπρακτον κεῖσθαι καὶ ἀνενέργητον· ἀλλ' ἐπὶ Θεὸν κατα φεύγειν, ὃς εἰ χελιδόνι τὰ τηλικαῦτα χαρίζεται, πόσῳ μείζονα δώσει τοῖς ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας ἐπιβοωμένοις αὐτόν; Ἁλκυών ἐστι θαλάττιον ὄρνεον. Αὕτη παρ' αὐτοὺς νοσσεύειν τοὺς αἰγιαλοὺς πέφυκεν, ἐπ' αὐτῆς τὰ ὠὰ τῆς ψάμμου καταθεμένη· καὶ νοσσεύει κατὰ μέσον που τὸν χειμῶνα, ὅτε πολλοῖς καὶ βιαίοις ἀνέμοις ἡ θάλασσα τῇ γῇ προσαράσσεται. Ἀλλ' ὅμως κοιμίζονται μὲν πάντες ἄνεμοι, ἡσυχάζει δὲ κῦμα θαλάσσιον, ὅταν ἁλκυὼν ἐπωάζῃ τὰς ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας. Ἐν τοσαύταις γὰρ μόναις ἐκλεπίζει τοὺς νεοττούς. Ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τροφῆς αὐτοῖς χρεία, ἄλλας ἑπτὰ πρὸς τὴν τῶν νεοττῶν αὔξησιν ὁ μεγαλόδωρος Θεὸς τῷ μικροτάτῳ ζῴῳ παρέσχετο. Ὥστε καὶ ναυτικοὶ πάντες ἴσασι τοῦτο, καὶ ἁλκυονίδας τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας προσαγορεύουσι. Ταῦτά σοι εἰς προτροπὴν τοῦ αἰτεῖν παρὰ Θεοῦ τὰ πρὸς σωτη ρίαν διὰ τῆς περὶ τὰ ἄλογα τοῦ Θεοῦ προνοίας νενομοθέτηται. Τί οὐκ ἂν γένοιτο τῶν παραδόξων ἕνεκεν σοῦ, ὃς κατ' εἰκόνα γέγονας τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅπουγε ὑπὲρ ὄρνιθος οὕτω μικρᾶς ἡ μεγάλη καὶ φοβερὰ κατέχεται θάλασσα, ἐν μέσῳ χειμῶνι γαλήνην ἄγειν ἐπιταχθεῖσα; 8.6 Τὴν τρυγόνα φασὶ διαζευχθεῖσάν ποτε τοῦ ὁμόζυγος, μηκέτι τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον καταδέχεσθαι κοινωνίαν, ἀλλὰ μένειν ἀσυνδύαστον, μνήμῃ τοῦ ποτὲ συζευχθέντος τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον κοινωνίαν ἀπαρνουμένην. Ἀκουέτωσαν αἱ γυναῖκες, ὅπως τὸ σεμνὸν τῆς χηρείας, καὶ παρὰ τοῖς ἀλόγοις, τοῦ ἐν ταῖς πολυγαμίαις ἀπρεποῦς προτιμότερον. Ἀδικώτατος περὶ τὴν τῶν ἐκγόνων ἐκτροφὴν ὁ ἀετός. Δύο γὰρ ἐξαγαγὼν νεοσσοὺς, τὸν ἕτερον αὐτῶν εἰς γῆν καταρρήγνυσι, ταῖς πληγαῖς τῶν πτερῶν ἀπωθούμενος· τὸν δὲ ἕτερον μόνον ἀναλαβὼν, οἰκειοῦται, διὰ τὸ τῆς τροφῆς ἐπίπονον ἀποποιούμενος ὃν ἐγέννησεν.
thought_title: Birds as moral teachers: hospitality, care for parents, poverty, and providence
orientation: Basil continues his survey of bird behavior, drawing moral lessons for his congregation from the stork, swallow, halcyon, turtledove, and eagle.
pass_a_gloss: Who among them defined the laws of hospitality? Who threatened them with a charge of desertion, so that not one is left behind from the escort? Let the inhospitable hear, those who shut their doors and do not share even shelter in winter and night with visitors. The care for the aged among the storks would have been enough to make our children lovers of their fathers, if they were willing to pay attention. For in every way no one is so lacking in understanding as not to judge it worthy of shame to fall short of the most irrational birds in virtue. Those birds, standing around in a circle, warm with their own feathers the father who has shed his feathers because of old age, and preparing food abundantly, they provide the help possible also in flight, gently lightening him on each side with the wing. And this is so celebrated among all that already some call the repayment of benefits 'antipelargosis.' Let no one lament poverty; let no one despair of his own life, the one who has left behind no property at home, looking at the resourcefulness of the swallow. For that bird, when building her nest, carries the twigs with her mouth; but not being able to lift mud with her feet, she wets the tips of her wings with water, then rolls them in the finest dust, and so she devises the use of mud; and binding the twigs to one another little by little with the mud as with some glue, she raises her young in it; if someone pierces their eyes, she has some healing from nature, through which she brings back the sight of her offspring to health. Let these things admonish you, not to turn to wickedness because of poverty; nor, having cast away all hope in the most difficult sufferings, to lie idle and inactive; but to flee to God, who if he grants such great things to a swallow, how much greater things will he give to those who call upon him from the whole heart? The halcyon is a sea bird. This bird is by nature accustomed to nest on the very shores, placing her eggs on the sand itself; and she nests around the middle of winter, when the sea dashes against the land with many violent winds. But nevertheless all winds are lulled to sleep, and the sea wave is still, whenever the halcyon broods for the seven days. For in only so many days she hatches her young. And since they also need food, the great-gifted God granted another seven days to the smallest creature for the growth of the young. So that all sailors know this, and they call those days 'halcyon days.' These things have been ordained for you as an encouragement to ask from God the things for salvation through God's providence for the irrational creatures. What would not happen of the marvelous things for your sake, you who have been made according to the image of God, when indeed for the sake of a bird so small the great and fearful sea is held back, ordered to keep calm in the middle of winter? They say that the turtledove, once separated from her mate, no longer accepts union with another, but remains unpaired, refusing union with another in memory of the one once joined. Let the women hear, how the dignity of widowhood, even among the irrational creatures, is more honorable than the indecency in polygamy. The eagle is most unjust concerning the rearing of its offspring. For having brought out two young, he dashes one of them to the ground, pushing it away with blows of his wings; and taking up only the other one, he makes it his own, rejecting because of the labor of feeding the one he begot.

choices.why: The term is a military legal charge for abandoning one's post; Basil uses it metaphorically for the cranes' escort duty.
Basil explicitly notes that 'some' use this coined term for repaying benefits, modeled on the stork (pelargos); keeping the transliteration preserves the wordplay.
εὐμήχανον means clever contrivance or ingenuity; 'resourcefulness' captures the inventive quality Basil praises.
This is the standard English idiom for the calm winter days, and Basil explicitly says sailors call them this.
σεμνόν carries a sense of solemn dignity and honor; 'dignity' fits Basil's moral contrast with polygamy.
The verb means to break or dash down violently; it conveys the eagle's forceful rejection of one chick.

pass_b_english: Who defined the laws of hospitality among them? Who threatened them with a charge of desertion, so that not one of them fails to join the escort? Let the inhospitable listen—those who shut their doors and do not even share a roof with travelers in winter and at night. The care storks show for their aged parents would be enough to make our children lovers of their fathers, if they were willing to pay attention. For surely no one is so lacking in understanding as to think it not worthy of shame to fall behind the most irrational birds in virtue. When the father has shed his feathers from old age, they stand around him in a circle and warm him with their own feathers, and they provide food in abundance, and they give him all the help they can in flight, gently lifting him on either side with their wings. And this is so widely celebrated that some people already call the repayment of benefits 'antipelargosis.' Let no one lament poverty; let no one despair of his life who has left no wealth at home, when he looks at the swallow's ingenuity. For when she builds her nest, she carries the twigs in her mouth; and since she cannot lift mud with her feet, she wets the tips of her wings with water, then rolls them in the finest dust, and in this way she devises the use of mud. And little by little she binds the twigs together with the mud as with a kind of glue, and in it she raises her young. If someone pierces out their eyes, she has a certain healing remedy from nature, through which she restores the sight of her offspring to health. Let these things admonish you not to turn to wickedness because of poverty, and not to cast away all hope in the most grievous sufferings and lie idle and inactive, but to flee to God—who, if he grants such great things to the swallow, how much greater things will he give to those who call upon him from a whole heart? The halcyon is a sea bird. It naturally nests on the very shores, laying its eggs on the sand itself; and it nests around the middle of winter, when the sea is dashed against the land by many violent winds. But nevertheless all the winds are lulled to sleep, and the sea wave is still, whenever the halcyon broods for the seven days. For in only so many days it hatches out its young. And since they also need food, the God who gives great gifts granted another seven days to the smallest creature for the growth of the young. So all sailors know this, and they call those days the halcyon days. These things have been ordained for you as an encouragement to ask God for the things that lead to salvation, through God's providence for the irrational creatures. What paradoxical thing would not happen for your sake, you who have been made according to the image of God, when for the sake of so small a bird the great and fearful sea is held back, commanded to keep calm in the middle of winter? 8.6 They say that the turtledove, once separated from her mate, no longer accepts union with another, but remains unpaired, refusing union with another out of memory of the one to whom she was once joined. Let women hear how the dignity of widowhood is preferred, even among irrational creatures, to the indecency of polygamy. The eagle is most unjust in the rearing of its young. For when it has brought out two chicks, it dashes one of them down to the ground, thrusting it away with blows of its wings; and taking up only the other one, it makes it its own, rejecting the one it begat because of the painful toil of feeding.

problems.why: εὐμήχανον is neuter noun 'ingenuity/devicefulness,' not just 'resourcefulness' as a quality; it's the thing itself

problems.quote: rejecting the one it begot because of the labor of feeding it
problems.source_quote: διὰ τὸ τῆς τροφῆς ἐπίπονον ἀποποιούμενος ὃν ἐγέννησεν
problems.why: ἀποποιούμενος is 'disowning/repudiating,' stronger than 'rejecting'; and ἐπίπονον is 'toilsome/painful,' not just 'labor'
problems.fix: disowning the one it begot because of the painful toil of feeding

edits.old: rejecting the one it begot because of the labor of feeding it
edits.new: disowning the one it begot because of the painful toil of feeding

fixed: Changed 'the resourcefulness of the swallow' to 'the swallow's ingenuity' to reflect εὐμήχανον as a neuter noun meaning ingenuity/devicefulness.
Changed 'rejecting' to 'disowning' and 'labor' to 'painful toil' to reflect ἀποποιούμενος and ἐπίπονον.

problems.quote: disowning the one it begot because of the painful toil of feeding
problems.source_quote: διὰ τὸ τῆς τροφῆς ἐπίπονον ἀποποιούμενος ὃν ἐγέννησεν
problems.why: ἀποποιούμενος means 'rejecting/disowning,' but the syntax shows the eagle disowns the rejected chick, not that it disowns 'because of painful toil' as a separate act. The phrase διὰ τὸ τῆς τροφῆς ἐπίπονον modifies the rejection: 'rejecting the one it begat on account of the labor of feeding.' The English makes 'disowning' a separate participial act rather than the main rejection.
problems.fix: taking up only the other, it claims that one as its own, rejecting the one it begat because of the painful labor of feeding

edits.old: and taking up only the other one, it makes it its own, disowning the one it begot because of the painful toil of feeding.
edits.new: and taking up only the other one, it makes it its own, rejecting the one it begat because of the painful toil of feeding.

fixed: The English 'disowning the one it begot because of the painful toil of feeding' misstates the source syntax. The source 'ἀποποιούμενος ὃν ἐγέννησεν' means 'rejecting the one it begat,' with 'διὰ τὸ τῆς τροφῆς ἐπίπονον' modifying the rejection. Changed 'disowning' to 'rejecting' and 'begot' to 'begat' to match the source participle and verb form.

last_rejected.quote: The care storks show for their aged parents would be enough to make our children lovers of their fathers
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἡ δὲ περὶ τοὺς γηράσαντας τῶν πελαργῶν πρόνοια ἐξήρκει τοὺς παῖδας ἡμῶν, εἰ προσέχειν ἐβούλοντο, φιλοπάτορας καταστῆσαι.
last_rejected.why: English drops the conditional 'if they were willing to pay attention' (εἰ προσέχειν ἐβούλοντο), changing a conditional into a flat assertion.
last_rejected.fix: The care storks show for their aged parents would be enough to make our children lovers of their fathers, if they were willing to pay attention.
last_rejected.ruling: English includes 'if they were willing to pay attention'—the conditional is present, not dropped.

last_rejected.quote: she devises the use of mud
last_rejected.source_quote: οὕτως ἐπινοεῖ τοῦ πηλοῦ τὴν χρείαν
last_rejected.why: Source says she 'devises the need/use for mud'—i.e., figures out how to use mud. English 'the use of mud' loses the ingenuity sense.
last_rejected.fix: in this way she figures out how to make use of mud
last_rejected.ruling: 'Devises the use of mud' captures ἐπινοεῖ τὴν χρείαν: she figures out how to employ mud; ingenuity is clear from context.

last_rejected.quote: refusing union with another out of memory of the one to whom she was once joined
last_rejected.source_quote: μνήμῃ τοῦ ποτὲ συζευχθέντος τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον κοινωνίαν ἀπαρνουμένην
last_rejected.why: Source says 'in memory of the one once joined to her' (τοῦ ποτὲ συζευχθέντος = the male). English 'the one to whom she was once joined' reverses agency.
last_rejected.fix: refusing union with another in memory of the one once joined to her
last_rejected.ruling: συζευχθέντος is passive aorist participle; 'to whom she was once joined' correctly renders passive with reversed English agency.

last_rejected.quote: not to cast away all hope in the most grievous sufferings and lie idle and inactive
last_rejected.source_quote: μηδὲ ἐν τοῖς χαλεπωτάτοις πάθεσι πᾶσαν ἐλπίδα ῥίψαντα, ἄπρακτον κεῖσθαι καὶ ἀνενέργητον
last_rejected.why: English adds 'lie idle and inactive' as if describing a person, but Greek describes hope (ἐλπίδα) cast away as inactive/ineffective.
last_rejected.fix: and not to cast away all hope in the most grievous sufferings, leaving it idle and ineffective
last_rejected.ruling: ἄπρακτον κεῖσθαι καὶ ἀνενέργητον are accusative participles agreeing with ῥίψαντα, describing the person, not hope.
